content:
Yesterday we saw how Korah's rebellion began and gathered others. We may read Numbers 16 and think, I would never stand before Moses with a censer, I would never gather two hundred and fifty men against Aaron. But the spirit that produced Korah's rebellion can appear much more quietly in us. It begins with comparison. Someone else receives a responsibility. Someone else is appreciated. Someone else teaches. Someone else is trusted with something important. Someone else's gift becomes visible. And something whispers within us, "Why them?" That question must be dealt with quickly, for Paul writes, "But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body just as He pleased" (1 Corinthians 12:18). God assigns gifts, callings, seasons, and roles, and when we continually fight His assignment, jealousy can develop into rebellion. So, the New Creation should learn to say, "Father, if this is the place You have given me, let me serve faithfully here." The hand does not need to become the eye. The eye does not need to become the foot. The Kohathite did not need to become the priest. Faithfulness is not becoming somebody else. Faithfulness is doing well what Yahweh has entrusted to us.

This same danger can quietly enter a congregation. Someone becomes offended by a brother, an elder, a teacher, or another member. And instead of speaking honestly and seeking peace, he begins speaking privately to others. "Did you notice what he did?" "I don't agree with how they are doing this." "Many people feel the same way." "Why should that person have that responsibility?"
One conversation becomes five conversations, and soon people are no longer discussing truth; they are gathering around dissatisfaction. Now this does not mean that leaders can never be questioned or corrected, for Scripture does not teach blind loyalty to human beings, and sin and false teaching must be addressed according to the Word. The issue with Korah was different: Yahweh had clearly appointed the order he was attacking, and his own ambition was hidden underneath his complaint. So before spreading a complaint, the New Creation should ask one searching question: am I trying to correct something according to Yahweh's Word, or am I simply trying to gather people to my side? That single question can save a congregation from much pain. Acts 20 warns that people can arise even from among ourselves and draw disciples after themselves (Acts 20:30), and internal pride, bitterness, and division can become far greater dangers to the church than any opposition from outside.

The same principle reaches into the world around us, and so we choose our friendships carefully, for Scripture says, "Do not be deceived: Evil company corrupts good habits" (1 Corinthians 15:33). Suppose we continually surround ourselves with people who mock holiness, make light of immorality, ridicule Scripture, encourage bitterness, or teach us to despise obedience. At first, we may say, "They are only my friends." But voices become thoughts, thoughts become attitudes, attitudes become choices, and choices become habits. Eventually we may discover that the people who were once simply around us have begun to shape the person within us. Proverbs says, "He who walks with wise men will be wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed" (Proverbs 13:20). This does not mean we refuse to love unbelievers, for Christ Himself loved sinners. But there is a great difference between loving someone and allowing that person's rebellious character to become our counsellor. Korah gathered companions who strengthened his rebellion; the New Creation needs companions who strengthen faith.

But there is an even deeper danger than gathering people outside us. We may never gather two hundred and fifty people, yet we can gather two hundred and fifty arguments inside our own head against Yahweh. God's Word tells us something clearly, but we do not like it, and so the mind begins gathering reasons. "Maybe God does not really require this." "Other Christians do it." "Times have changed." "This command is too difficult." "I deserve this." "Surely this one compromise will not matter." Soon we have built an entire congregation of arguments inside our own mind, all of them agreeing with what our flesh already wanted. That is Korah's principle working inwardly. Paul therefore tells us to be "bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5). We must not allow rebellious thoughts to hold their meetings in our mind. When the Word of Yahweh exposes us, the New Creation does not gather arguments against it.
We surrender, and we say, "Yes, Father. Your Word is right. Change me."That is the very opposite of Korah.

And we must remember that Korah was judged. Moses did not need to destroy Korah to protect his own position. He simply placed the matter before Yahweh, and in time Yahweh judged. The earth opened and those connected with the rebellion went down into it, and fire came from Yahweh and consumed the two hundred and fifty men who had presumptuously offered incense (Numbers 16:31-35). The judgment was terrible because the rebellion was serious. God's fatherhood does not cancel His holiness; the Father is also the Judge. The New Testament warns, "Do not be deceived, God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7), and Jude specifically remembers those who "perished in the rebellion of Korah" (Jude 11). So Korah remains a warning even for us.

How then do we avoid becoming like Korah? First, we must be thankful for Yahweh's assignment, and instead of asking, "Why did God give that person more?" we ask, "How faithfully am I using what God gave me?" Second, we must stop comparison quickly, for comparison feeds jealousy, and jealousy can eventually make another person's blessing feel like our own injury. Third, we must not gather people around personal bitterness; if there is a genuine problem, we handle it truthfully and peacefully, and do not recruit supporters simply to strengthen our side. Fourth, we must choose our companions carefully, so that our closest voices encourage obedience, holiness, and humility, rather than continually feeding anger, pride, and rebellion. Fifth, we must watch the private conversation inside the mind, for before Korah gathered two hundred and fifty men outside himself, rebellion had already gathered its thoughts inside him. So, we pray like David, "Search me, O God, and know my heart... and see if there is any wicked way in me" (Psalm 139:23-24). And finally, we must remain under Christ our Head, for Messiah is the Head of the body, and when the Head is honoured, the body walks in order. So, the cure for Korah's spirit is not to become passive. It is to become humble. Let us serve where Yahweh places us, be faithful with what He gives us, celebrate another's usefulness, correct wrong according to Scripture without creating factions, and choose friends who strengthen our new life. Korah's downfall did not begin when the earth opened. It began much earlier, when the holy responsibility God had given him became a small thing in his own eyes. May we never despise the place Yahweh gives us, nor gather others around our bitterness, but remain humbly under Christ our Head, remembering that the brother is meant to be our help and not our competition, and that Yahweh's assignment is always safer than the position our pride desires.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God, who sets each member in the body just as You please,
Make us thankful for the place You have given us, and quick to stop every comparison.

Guard our friendships, and let our closest voices strengthen our faith, not our flesh.

Do not let rebellious thoughts gather and hold their meetings within our minds.

When Your Word exposes us, help us not to argue, but to surrender and say, 'Change me.'

Keep us humble and faithful under Christ our Head, serving gladly where You have placed us.

"Search me, O God, and know my heart, and see if there is any offensive way in me." Psalm 139:23-24

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
